{{Short description|Statement in probability theory}}
[[File:Donskers invariance principle.gif|thumb|Donsker's invariance principle for [[simple random walk]] on <math>\mathbb Z</math>.]]
In [[probability theory]], '''Donsker's theorem''' (also known as '''Donsker's invariance principle''', or the '''functional central limit theorem'''), named after [[Monroe D. Donsker]], is a functional extension of the [[central limit theorem]] for empirical distribution functions. Specifically, the theorem states that an appropriately centered and scaled version of the empirical distribution function converges to a [[Gaussian process]]. 

Let <math>X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots</math> be a sequence of [[Independent and identically distributed random variables|independent and identically distributed]] (i.i.d.) [[Random variable|random variables]] with mean 0 and variance 1. Let <math>S_n:=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i</math>. The stochastic process <math>S:=(S_n)_{n\in\N}</math> is known as a [[random walk]]. Define the diffusively rescaled random walk (partial-sum process) by

: <math>W^{(n)}(t) := \frac{S_{\lfloor nt\rfloor}}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad t\in [0,1].</math>

The [[central limit theorem]] asserts that <math>W^{(n)}(1)</math> [[converges in distribution]] to a standard [[Gaussian random variable]] <math>W(1)</math> as <math>n\to\infty</math>. Donsker's invariance principle<ref>{{Cite journal|title = An invariance principle for certain probability limit theorems|last = Donsker|first = M.D.|journal = Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society |year=1951 |issue=6 |author-link= Monroe D. Donsker |mr=0040613}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> extends this convergence to the whole function <math>W^{(n)}:=(W^{(n)}(t))_{t\in [0,1]}</math>. More precisely, in its modern form, Donsker's invariance principle states that: As [[Random variable|random variables]] taking values in the [[Skorokhod space]] <math>\mathcal{D}[0,1]</math>, the random function <math>W^{(n)}</math> [[converges in distribution]] to a [[Wiener process|standard Brownian motion]] <math>W:=(W(t))_{t\in [0,1]}</math> as <math>n\to \infty.</math>
[[File:Donsker_theorem_for_uniform_distributions.gif|thumb|Donsker-Skorokhod-Kolmogorov theorem for uniform distributions.]]
[[File:Donsker_theorem_for_normal_distributions.gif|thumb|Donsker-Skorokhod-Kolmogorov theorem for normal distributions]]

==Formal statement==
Let ''F''<sub>''n''</sub> be the [[empirical distribution function]] of the sequence of i.i.d. random variables  <math>X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots</math> with distribution function ''F.'' Define the centered and scaled version of ''F''<sub>''n''</sub> by

: <math> G_n(x)= \sqrt n ( F_n(x) - F(x) ) </math>

indexed by ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''. By the classical [[central limit theorem]], for fixed ''x'', the random variable ''G''<sub>''n''</sub>(''x'') [[converges in distribution]] to a [[normal distribution|Gaussian (normal)]] [[random variable]] ''G''(''x'') with zero mean and variance ''F''(''x'')(1&nbsp;−&nbsp;''F''(''x'')) as the sample size ''n'' grows.

'''Theorem''' (Donsker, Skorokhod, Kolmogorov) The sequence of ''G''<sub>''n''</sub>(''x''), as random elements of the [[Skorokhod space]] <math>\mathcal{D}(-\infty,\infty)</math>, [[convergence in distribution|converges in distribution]] to a [[Gaussian process]] ''G'' with zero mean and covariance given by

: <math>\operatorname{cov}[G(s), G(t)] = E[G(s) G(t)] = \min\{F(s), F(t)\} - F(s)</math><math>{F}(t). </math>

The process ''G''(''x'') can be written as ''B''(''F''(''x'')) where ''B'' is a standard [[Brownian bridge]] on the [[unit interval]].

=== Proof sketch ===
For continuous probability distributions, it reduces to the case where the distribution is uniform on <math>[0, 1] </math> by the [[Inverse transform sampling|inverse transform]].

Given any finite sequence of times <math>0 < t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_n < 1</math>, we have that <math>N F_N(t_1)</math> is distributed as a [[binomial distribution]] with mean <math>Nt_1 </math> and variance <math>Nt_1(1-t_1) </math>. 

Similarly, the joint distribution of <math>F_N(t_1), F_N(t_2), \dots, F_N(t_n)</math> is a multinomial distribution. Now, the [[Multinomial distribution#Asymptotics|central limit approximation for multinomial distributions]] shows that <math>\lim_N \sqrt N (F_N(t_i) - t_i) </math> converges in distribution to a gaussian process with covariance matrix with entries <math>\min(t_i, t_j) - t_i t_j </math>, which is precisely the covariance matrix for the Brownian bridge.

== History and related results ==
Kolmogorov (1933) showed that when ''F'' is [[continuous function|continuous]], the supremum <math>\scriptstyle\sup_t G_n(t)</math> and supremum of absolute value, <math>\scriptstyle\sup_t |G_n(t)|</math> [[convergence in distribution|converges in distribution]] to the laws of the same functionals of the [[Brownian bridge]] ''B''(''t''), see the [[Kolmogorov–Smirnov test]]. In 1949 Doob asked whether the convergence in distribution held for more general functionals, thus formulating a problem of [[weak convergence of measures|weak convergence]] of random functions in a suitable [[function space]].<ref>{{cite journal
 |first=Joseph L. |last=Doob|author-link=Joseph L. Doob
 |title=Heuristic approach to the Kolmogorov–Smirnov theorems
 |journal=[[Annals of Mathematical Statistics]]
 |volume=20 |issue= 3|pages=393–403 |year=1949
 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177729991 |mr=30732 | zbl = 0035.08901
|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 1952 Donsker stated and proved (not quite correctly)<ref name="dudley1999">{{cite book
 |first=R.M. |last=Dudley|author-link=Richard M. Dudley
 |title=Uniform Central Limit Theorems
 |publisher=Cambridge University Press
 |year=1999
 |isbn=978-0-521-46102-3
}}</ref> a general extension for the Doob–Kolmogorov heuristic approach. In the original paper, Donsker proved that the convergence in law of ''G''<sub>''n''</sub> to the Brownian bridge holds for [[uniform distribution (continuous)|Uniform[0,1]]] distributions with respect to [[uniform convergence]] in ''t'' over the interval [0,1].<ref name=":0">{{cite journal
 |first=M. D. |last=Donsker |author-link=Monroe D. Donsker
 |title=Justification and extension of Doob's heuristic approach to the Kolmogorov–Smirnov theorems
 |journal=[[Annals of Mathematical Statistics]]
 |volume=23 |issue= 2|pages=277–281 |year=1952
 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177729445 |mr=47288 | zbl = 0046.35103
|doi-access=free}}</ref>

However Donsker's formulation was not quite correct because of the problem of measurability of the functionals of discontinuous processes. In 1956 Skorokhod and Kolmogorov defined a separable metric ''d'', called the ''Skorokhod metric'', on the space of [[càdlàg]] functions on [0,1], such that convergence for ''d'' to a continuous function is equivalent to convergence for the sup norm, and showed that ''G<sub>n</sub>'' converges in law in <math>\mathcal{D}[0,1]</math> to the Brownian bridge.

Later Dudley reformulated Donsker's result to avoid the problem of measurability and the need of the Skorokhod metric. One can prove<ref name="dudley1999" /> that there exist ''X''<sub>''i''</sub>, iid uniform in [0,1] and a sequence of sample-continuous Brownian bridges ''B''<sub>''n''</sub>, such that
:<math>\|G_n-B_n\|_\infty</math>
is measurable and [[convergence in probability|converges in probability]] to 0. An improved version of this result, providing more detail on the [[rate of convergence]], is the [[Komlós–Major–Tusnády approximation]].
